## Module Overview

Imagine you are building a semantic search engine and want queries like “Seattle motel” to return documents about “Seattle hotel” even if “motel” never appears in them. With one-hot word representations, these words are orthogonal and have no notion of similarity, so the system fails to generalize. Skip-gram Word Embeddings (the core of Word2Vec) solve this by learning dense vectors from large corpora such that words appearing in similar contexts get similar representations. In industry, this idea underpins everything from legacy search and recommendation systems to how modern Transformer models are first motivated and understood. Beyond your coursework, this module will give you a more practice-ready understanding of how skip-gram is actually scaled and used, and how it connects to subword models that are still influential today. How do we go from the elegant softmax objective you saw in class to something that can train on billions of tokens in practice?

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this module, you will be able to:

1. **Explain** how the skip-gram model represents words with center vectors \(v_w\) and context vectors \(u_w\), and how it uses dot-product similarity and a softmax over the vocabulary to predict context words. (Curriculum)  
2. **Derive** the conditional probability \(P(o \mid c)\) in the skip-gram model and **describe** how stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is used to optimize the embeddings on large corpora. (Curriculum)  
3. **Implement and tune** a skip-gram-style training pipeline that uses scalable softmax approximations (e.g., negative sampling) to learn useful embeddings from realistic corpora. (Gap)  
4. **Analyze and compare** word representations produced by word-level skip-gram versus subword/character n‑gram extensions (fastText-style) for rare and morphologically rich words. (Gap)  
5. **Evaluate** when to prefer basic skip-gram embeddings versus subword skip-gram variants in an industry setting, given constraints such as vocabulary size, language morphology, and downstream task. (Gap)

## Curriculum Coverage

In the course, you learned that representing words as one-hot vectors leads to orthogonal representations with no intrinsic notion of similarity—“motel” and “hotel” are as far apart as any unrelated pair of words. To address this, the curriculum introduces distributional semantics: “you shall know a word by the company it keeps.” A word’s meaning is represented by the words that frequently appear near it in text. From this starting point, the course presents dense word vectors (embeddings) as distributed representations that capture similarity via their positions in a continuous vector space.

The curriculum then introduces Word2Vec, specifically the skip-gram model, as a framework for learning such vectors from a large corpus. Every word in a fixed vocabulary gets two dense vectors: a center (input) vector \(v_w\) and a context (output) vector \(u_w\). At each position \(t\) in the text, with center word \(c = w_t\), the model is trained to predict surrounding context words \(o\) within a fixed window (e.g., words at positions \(t-2, t-1, t+1, t+2\)). The probability of a particular context word \(o\) given center word \(c\) is modeled via a softmax over the vocabulary using the dot product similarity \(u_o^\top v_c\) as a score. The parameters \(v_w\) and \(u_w\) are optimized with stochastic gradient descent (SGD), iterating over the corpus and adjusting vectors to maximize the likelihood of observed context words.

Overall, the course emphasizes the mathematical form of the skip-gram objective, the two-vector parameterization, and the role of dot-product similarity and softmax in turning vector similarity into probabilities. It focuses on conceptual understanding and gradient-based optimization basics rather than engineering details, leaving out many of the approximations and heuristics used in large-scale industry systems.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What are the center and context vectors (\(v_w\) and \(u_w\)) in skip-gram, and why do we need both?  
- How is the probability \(P(o \mid c)\) defined using the dot product \(u_o^\top v_c\) and a softmax over the vocabulary?  
- How does SGD use training examples of \((\text{center}, \text{context})\) pairs to update the word vectors?

## Identified Gaps

The curriculum gives you a solid conceptual foundation of skip-gram: two-vector parameterization, dot-product similarity, softmax over the vocabulary, and SGD optimization. However, it largely assumes an idealized setting where the full softmax can be computed and does not cover the practical approximations needed to scale training to large corpora and vocabularies. (Critical) In industry, negative sampling and related tricks are standard, and being able to implement and tune these is often essential for working with legacy embedding pipelines or understanding older components in larger systems.

Another major gap is the treatment of subword information. While the course later introduces subword modeling (e.g., byte-pair encoding and WordPiece) in the context of modern pretrained Transformer models, it does not connect this back to skip-gram-style training for static word embeddings. (Critical) Industry frequently uses subword or character n‑gram extensions (fastText-style) built on top of the skip-gram idea to handle rare words and morphologically complex languages.

Additional gaps include: practical training heuristics (e.g., negative sampling distributions, subsampling frequent words), evaluation and selection of embeddings for real tasks, and details on how these static embeddings relate to later contextual models. (Important) In this module, we focus primarily on scalable training (negative sampling) and subword skip-gram (fastText-style), since these are the highest-priority skills for employability and for understanding how dense word embeddings connect to modern NLP pipelines.

## Core Content

### What You Need to Learn

We will focus on two critical gap areas:

1. Scalable skip-gram training using negative sampling.  
2. Subword / character n‑gram extensions of skip-gram (fastText-style).

#### 1. Scalable Training: Negative Sampling for Skip-gram

Building on the softmax-based skip-gram objective you studied, industry must deal with the fact that computing a softmax over a very large vocabulary (hundreds of thousands or millions of words) is computationally expensive at every training step. Negative sampling is a practical workaround that preserves the core idea—making observed \((c, o)\) pairs likely—while avoiding the full softmax normalization.

**Definition (Negative Sampling).** Instead of modeling a full probability distribution over the vocabulary for each center word, negative sampling turns each observed \((c, o)\) pair into a small binary classification problem:  
- The observed context word \(o\) is a *positive* example for center \(c\).  
- A small set of words sampled from the vocabulary (the “negative samples”) are treated as *negative* examples—words that should *not* occur in the context of \(c\) for this training instance.

For each training pair \((c, o)\), the model:
- Increases the dot product \(u_o^\top v_c\) so that the positive word looks more likely.  
- Decreases the dot products \(u_{n_i}^\top v_c\) for sampled negative words \(n_i\), pushing them away from the center vector.

While the detailed loss formulas are beyond what we need here, conceptually you are still using the same parameters \(v_w\) and \(u_w\) and the same dot-product similarity, but replacing the global softmax with a local, sampled objective.

**Step-by-step application in training**

Given you already know how to generate \((c, o)\) pairs from sliding windows:

1. **Prepare training data.**  
   - From your corpus, construct all \((\text{center}, \text{context})\) pairs within a window, exactly as in full softmax skip-gram.  
   - Build a frequency-based distribution over vocabulary words (a unigram distribution), which will be used to draw negatives.

2. **For each positive pair \((c, o)\):**  
   1. Sample a small number \(k\) of negative words \(\{n_1, \dots, n_k\}\) from the vocabulary using a noise distribution based on word frequencies.  
   2. Compute the dot product for the positive pair \(u_o^\top v_c\).  
   3. Compute the dot products for each negative pair \(u_{n_i}^\top v_c\).  
   4. Update \(v_c\), \(u_o\), and the \(u_{n_i}\) using SGD to:  
      - Increase similarity for the positive pair.  
      - Decrease similarity for the negatives.

3. **Repeat across corpus.**  
   - Iterate over the corpus for multiple epochs, continuing to draw fresh negative samples for each positive pair.  
   - Because you only touch a handful of vectors per training step (the center, one positive context, and a few negatives), training scales much better than with a full softmax.

**Industry example.**  
Many production systems that predate large Transformers still rely on Word2Vec-style embeddings trained with negative sampling. For example, a legacy recommendation system might represent items and queries in a shared embedding space using skip-gram with negative sampling, then compute dot products (or cosine similarity) for retrieval. Negative sampling enables training these embeddings on billions of user interaction sequences where computing a full softmax would be impractical.

In practice, engineers tune:
- The number of negative samples \(k\) (e.g., a small integer).  
- The noise distribution used to draw negatives (commonly a smoothed unigram distribution).  
- Learning rate schedules and window sizes—conceptually similar to what you already know from SGD, but applied in a more scalable training loop.

#### 2. Subword / Character n‑gram Skip-gram (fastText-style)

Your course later discusses subword modeling (e.g., byte-pair encoding) to split words into smaller units so that rare forms can benefit from data associated with their parts. The same idea can be applied in the skip-gram setting to build more robust word embeddings, particularly for rare and morphologically complex words.

**Definition (Subword skip-gram).** Instead of assigning a single vector to each word and training skip-gram directly on word tokens, a subword skip-gram model represents each word as a combination of vectors for its character n‑grams (e.g., “ban”, “ank”, “nki”, “kin”, “ing” for “banking”). The word vector used in the skip-gram objective is then the sum or average of these n‑gram vectors. Training still uses the skip-gram objective (often with negative sampling), but the parameters correspond to subword units rather than just whole words.

**How it works conceptually**

- For every word, generate a set of character n‑grams.  
- Maintain vectors for all subword units (n‑grams).  
- When a word appears as a center or context word, compose its word vector by combining its subword vectors (e.g., summation).  
- Use this composed vector in the usual skip-gram training: predict context from center, adjusting subword vectors rather than just a single word-level vector.

**Step-by-step application in training**

1. **Define subword units.**  
   - Decide on an n‑gram range (e.g., 3–6 characters).  
   - For each word in the vocabulary, precompute its list of character n‑grams.

2. **Initialize subword vectors.**  
   - Assign a dense vector to each possible n‑gram (these are now your primary parameters, instead of just word-level \(v_w\) and \(u_w\)).  

3. **Build training pairs.**  
   - As before, slide a window over the corpus to construct \((\text{center}, \text{context})\) pairs at the word level.

4. **For each pair \((c, o)\):**  
   1. Compose the center vector \(v_c\) by adding or averaging the vectors of c’s n‑grams.  
   2. Compose the context vector \(u_o\) from o’s n‑grams (for a symmetric model) or maintain separate subword vectors for context if desired.  
   3. Apply a skip-gram training step (often with negative sampling) using these composed vectors:  
      - Increase similarity between the n‑gram-based representations of \(c\) and \(o\).  
      - Decrease similarity with n‑gram representations of negative samples.

5. **Inference for new words.**  
   - At test time, for an unseen word, you can still build a vector by splitting it into known n‑grams and combining their learned vectors—even if the full word never appeared in training.

**Industry example.**  
A multilingual search engine might use subword skip-gram embeddings to support languages with rich morphology (e.g., highly inflected languages). Rather than having separate unreliable embeddings for each rare inflected form, the system leverages shared subword pieces across forms, improving similarity estimates between related words and enabling reasonable embeddings for rare or even unseen forms.

This is particularly valuable when:
- The vocabulary is huge (many inflected or compound forms).  
- You expect many misspellings or user-generated variations.  
- You need robust behavior on rare but important terms.

#### Brief notes on remaining gaps

- **Evaluation and selection of embeddings.** You should know that embeddings can be evaluated both intrinsically (e.g., similarity/analogy tests) and extrinsically (performance on downstream tasks), and that analogy tests have limits; see the resources in Further Reading for practical guidance.  
- **Choosing vectors for downstream use.** In practice, people often use the “input” vectors (analogous to \(v_w\)) or an average of input and output vectors; normalization and cosine similarity are common choices.  
- **Theoretical links to matrix factorization and alternatives (e.g., GloVe).** Skip-gram with negative sampling can be seen as implicitly factorizing a word–context co-occurrence matrix; understanding this helps when comparing word2vec-style methods to global co-occurrence models.

You can explore these topics further via the references in the Further Reading section.

### Common Misconceptions

1. **Misconception:** “Negative sampling is a completely different model from skip-gram.”  
   - **Why it’s wrong:** Negative sampling does not change the core idea of skip-gram; it changes how the objective is approximated, not what the model is trying to capture.  
   - **Correct view:** Negative sampling is a training trick to avoid the full softmax, but the underlying representation (center/context vectors and dot products capturing similarity) remains the same.

2. **Misconception:** “Subword models replace word embeddings entirely, so word-level skip-gram is obsolete.”  
   - **Why it’s wrong:** Subword models *extend* skip-gram by composing word vectors from smaller units; they still rely on the same skip-gram training principle.  
   - **Correct view:** Subword skip-gram builds on word2vec-style training and is especially useful for rare and morphologically complex words, but the basic word-level formulation is still relevant and widely used as a conceptual and practical foundation.

3. **Misconception:** “Once embeddings are trained, using them is just about plugging in the vectors; no need to know how they were trained.”  
   - **Why it’s wrong:** Training choices (e.g., negative sampling, subword composition) directly affect what the vectors encode and when they will work well or fail.  
   - **Correct view:** Understanding training details is key to interpreting embedding behavior, diagnosing issues (e.g., poor rare-word performance), and making informed decisions about which pretrained embeddings to use.

## Industry Context

Roles that value a solid understanding of skip-gram word embeddings include:
- Machine Learning Engineer (NLP focus)  
- Data Scientist working on search/recommendation systems  
- NLP Engineer maintaining or modernizing legacy embedding-based pipelines

A typical real-world use case is in large-scale document retrieval or product recommendation. For example, an e-commerce platform might model user sessions as sequences of viewed products and train a skip-gram-with-negative-sampling model to learn embeddings where products frequently viewed together are close in vector space. These embeddings are then used to retrieve similar or complementary items using dot-product or cosine similarity, improving recommendation quality even for items that share few explicit metadata features. Subword extensions help capture similarity between products with rare or creative names by decomposing names into character n‑grams, improving robustness to spelling variations and new items entering the catalog.

Employers hiring for such roles look for candidates who can:  
- Explain the skip-gram objective and how word similarity emerges from distributional context.  
- Implement and tune scalable training (e.g., negative sampling, window sizes, learning rates) on large corpora.  
- Understand when to adopt subword models and how these interact with tokenization choices in broader NLP systems (including Transformers).  
- Evaluate embeddings quantitatively and qualitatively, and troubleshoot problems such as poor performance on rare words or domain-specific vocabulary.

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check

1. **What are the two vectors learned for each word in skip-gram, and what roles do they play?**  
   > Answer: Each word has a center (input) vector \(v_w\) used when the word is the center of a window, and a context (output) vector \(u_w\) used when the word appears as a surrounding context; their dot product scores how compatible a center–context pair is.

2. **How does the skip-gram model define the probability of a context word \(o\) given a center word \(c\)?**  
   > Answer: It uses a softmax over the vocabulary: \(P(o \mid c) = \frac{\exp(u_o^\top v_c)}{\sum_{w} \exp(u_w^\top v_c)}\), where the numerator is the exponentiated dot product between the center and the specific context vector, and the denominator sums over all vocabulary words.

3. **Conceptual (gap concept): What problem does negative sampling solve in skip-gram training, and how does it address it at a high level?**  
   > Answer: Negative sampling avoids computing a full softmax over a huge vocabulary; instead, it turns each observed center–context pair into a small binary classification problem by contrasting it against a handful of sampled negative words, updating only those few vectors per step.

4. **Application: Suppose you are training embeddings for a language with many inflected word forms. How would you combine skip-gram and subword modeling to better represent rare inflections?**  
   > Answer: Use a subword skip-gram approach where each word is represented as a combination (e.g., sum) of its character n‑gram vectors, then train with the skip-gram objective (likely with negative sampling); this shares parameters across related forms, improving representations for rare inflections.

### Apply It

Imagine you are tasked with improving search quality for a news website in a morphologically rich language. The site currently uses basic one-hot keyword matching and misses relevant articles when users type infrequent inflected forms or slightly misspelled words. You decide to introduce dense word embeddings learned from the site’s article corpus and user queries. However, you must scale training to millions of tokens and ensure that rare forms are still represented usefully.

Within this scenario:

- **Task 1:** Design a skip-gram-style training setup, specifying how you will construct center–context pairs and apply an efficient training objective (e.g., negative sampling).  
- **Task 2:** Propose a subword skip-gram strategy using character n‑grams to create embeddings that generalize across inflected and misspelled forms.  
- **Task 3:** Outline how you would evaluate whether the new embeddings improve search quality (e.g., simple quantitative or qualitative checks).  
- **Task 4:** Describe how you would integrate the learned word (or subword-composed) vectors into the existing search pipeline for ranking candidate articles.

**Expected outcome/deliverable:** A short technical design document (or notebook) that specifies the training procedure (including negative sampling), subword modeling choices, and evaluation measures, along with a clear description of how the learned embeddings would be used to compute similarity between user queries and article content.

## Key Takeaways

- **Curriculum:** One-hot word vectors are orthogonal and lack any built-in notion of similarity, motivating dense embeddings that encode similarity in the vectors themselves.  
- **Curriculum:** Skip-gram represents each word with two vectors, \(v_w\) (center) and \(u_w\) (context), learned jointly from large corpora.  
- **Curriculum:** The similarity between a center word \(c\) and a context word \(o\) is modeled via the dot product \(u_o^\top v_c\), which feeds into a softmax over the vocabulary to define \(P(o \mid c)\).  
- **Curriculum:** Training data for skip-gram consists of center–context pairs extracted from windows around each word position in the corpus.  
- **Curriculum:** Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is used to iteratively update word vectors to increase the probability of observed context words given their centers.

- **Gap:** Negative sampling replaces the expensive full softmax with a sampled objective that contrasts positive center–context pairs against a handful of negatives, enabling scalable training on large corpora.  
- **Gap:** Subword/character n‑gram extensions of skip-gram compose word vectors from smaller units, improving representations for rare, morphologically complex, and misspelled words.  
- **Gap:** Practical deployment requires understanding how training choices (sampling strategy, window size, subword granularity) affect embedding behavior on downstream tasks and in production systems.  
- **Gap:** Evaluating and selecting embeddings involves both intrinsic tests and downstream performance, and must be aligned with the specific application (e.g., search, recommendation).

- **Integration:** The mathematical skip-gram model you learned (center/context vectors, dot products, softmax, SGD) is the conceptual core that negative sampling and subword methods build on to achieve industrial-scale training.  
- **Integration:** Mastering both the theory (curriculum) and the practical approximations (gaps) enables you to understand legacy embedding systems and how they connect to modern, pretrained NLP models.

## Reflection

- What was the most important thing you learned in this module?  
- Which gap area do you feel least confident about? What would help you strengthen it?  
- How does Skip-gram Word Embeddings connect to other topics you have studied?

## Further Reading

- [Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (Mikolov et al., 2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781) (Research Paper) (Intermediate) – Introduces the original Word2Vec models, including skip-gram, and discusses efficient training strategies at a high level.  
- [Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality (Mikolov et al., 2013) — negative sampling details](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546) (Research Paper) (Advanced) – Provides more detail on negative sampling and practical heuristics for training skip-gram models on large corpora.  
- [word2vec Explained: deriving Mikolov et al.'s negative-sampling word-embedding method (Goldberg & Levy, 2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.3722) (Research Paper) (Advanced) – Offers a detailed derivation and analysis of skip-gram with negative sampling, useful for deep theoretical understanding.  
- [Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information (Bojanowski et al., 2017; fastText)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.04606) (Research Paper) (Intermediate) – Describes a subword-based extension of skip-gram that composes word vectors from character n‑grams, widely used in industry.  
- [fastText official site and pre-trained vectors](https://fasttext.cc/) (Documentation) (Beginner–Intermediate) – Provides tools and pretrained models for training and using subword skip-gram embeddings in practical applications.

Most students think they understand skip-gram once they’ve seen the softmax equation. But what if I told you that, in industry, that version basically never ships, and without one extra idea it simply doesn’t scale to real vocabularies?

You’ve already learned about skip-gram with center vectors v, context vectors u, a dot product between them, and a softmax that predicts nearby words using SGD. That’s a solid foundation, but there are two critical extensions your course didn’t really dig into: negative sampling to make training actually feasible, and subword skip-gram so rare and unseen words still get good embeddings.

Let’s start with negative sampling. Intuitively, instead of asking, “Given this center word, how probable is every word in the whole vocabulary?” we flip it into, “Given this center word, which words look like real neighbors and which look fake?” So each training step becomes a tiny binary classification game: one true context word versus a few randomly sampled “noise” words.

Why does this matter? A full softmax means, for every training pair, you touch every single word vector in the vocabulary. With hundreds of thousands of words and billions of tokens, that’s hopelessly slow. Negative sampling is the trick that lets Word2Vec-style models train at web scale on ordinary hardware.

Here’s how it works. For each observed center–context pair, say center “hotel” and context “Seattle”, you first treat that as a positive example. Then you sample k negative words from a noise distribution, often proportional to unigram frequency to the 0.75 power. That tends to pick common words, but not so aggressively that “the” dominates. If you’re looking at the slide, you can see the process flow: we start from the corpus pair, we sample negatives, we compute dot products, we apply a contrastive loss, and then we do an SGD update. Concretely, you increase the dot product u_Seattleᵀ v_hotel, pulling “Seattle” closer to “hotel,” and you decrease u_nᵀ v_hotel for each negative word n, pushing those away. The key insight is: you still have the same v and u vectors and the same notion of similarity via dot product — you’ve just replaced the expensive full softmax with a cheap sampled objective that only touches a handful of vectors per step.

Now let’s shift to subword skip-gram. Classic skip-gram gives each word its own vector. That breaks down for rare inflected forms, misspellings, and morphologically rich languages where you see thousands of variants of the same stem. Subword skip-gram fixes this by building a word’s embedding from character n‑grams, so words can share pieces. On the slide’s comparison diagram, instead of a single ID lookup for the whole word, you see the word broken into character n‑grams and then recomposed into a vector. For a word like “banking”, you might use 3–6 character n‑grams such as “ban”, “ank”, “nki”, “kin”, “ing”. You assign vectors to each of these n‑grams. To get the word vector for “banking”, you sum or average its n‑gram vectors. Then you plug that composed vector into the usual skip-gram training loop, typically with negative sampling. The model no longer learns “banking” in isolation; it learns reusable pieces that also appear in “bank”, “banker”, or “unbanked”. The key benefit is that a word you’ve never seen before can still get a meaningful embedding, as long as its character n‑grams were seen during training. That’s exactly why subword skip-gram, like fastText, is still widely used in production for noisy text, user queries, and morphologically rich languages.

Now, a lot of students hear about negative sampling and think, “Oh, that’s a different model — it replaces skip-gram.” But here’s the thing: it doesn’t change the representation or the goal at all. You still learn center and context vectors, and you still want high dot products for true neighbors and low ones for unrelated words. Negative sampling is just a scalable way to approximate the same objective without computing a full softmax.

Before I wrap up, pause for a moment and think about this: if you had to train embeddings on a billion-token corpus with lots of rare word forms, how would you combine negative sampling and subword skip-gram to make training both scalable and robust to those rare words?

So here’s what I want you to take away from this. First, negative sampling turns the softmax skip-gram objective into many tiny contrastive classification problems so you can train on massive vocabularies. Second, subword skip-gram composes word vectors from character n‑grams, giving good representations even for rare or unseen forms. And third, both ideas keep the original skip-gram core — center and context vectors, dot products, and SGD — but make it practical for real-world NLP. Mastering these puts you much closer to how embeddings are actually built and used in industry.

## Module Overview
Imagine you are building a search engine and a user types "Seattle motel" — you want the system to surface pages mentioning "Seattle hotel" even when the exact word "motel" and "hotel" are different tokens. Distributional semantics provides the foundation for encoding that graded similarity into dense vectors by using words' linguistic contexts. This topic matters now because industry systems rely on learned dense embeddings (and their extensions) for search relevance, recommendation, and downstream NLP models, and employers expect practical skills in training, evaluating, and adapting these vectors. In this module you will go beyond the course’s conceptual framing to learn the industry-relevant methods for training prediction-based embeddings, understand count-based alternatives and their connection to prediction models, and see how these choices affect OOV handling and deployment. Ready to turn the Firth adage into embeddings you can train, tune, and deploy?

## Learning Objectives
1. Explain the distributional semantics principle and how context windows produce dense vectors that encode graded similarity. (Curriculum)  
2. Describe why one-hot representations fail to capture similarity and why data-driven embeddings are preferred to fixed lexical resources like WordNet. (Curriculum)  
3. Implement and tune a prediction-based embedding pipeline (e.g., skip-gram with negative sampling), including choices for window size, negative sampling, subsampling, and embedding dimensionality. (Gap - Apply)  
4. Compare count-based approaches (co-occurrence + PPMI + SVD or GloVe) to prediction-based embeddings and analyze when each is preferable. (Gap - Analyze)  
5. Evaluate embedding quality using intrinsic (e.g., similarity benchmarks) and extrinsic (downstream task) diagnostics, and propose simple mitigation strategies for common OOV and bias issues. (Gap - Evaluate)

## Curriculum Coverage
The course material presents the classical distributional semantics idea: a word’s meaning is captured by the words that frequently appear nearby in text ("You shall know a word by the company it keeps"). It motivates moving away from discrete one-hot vectors (which are orthogonal and lack a natural notion of similarity) and away from brittle lexical resources like WordNet toward learned dense real-valued vectors that encode graded similarities in geometric space. The curriculum describes how contexts are defined (fixed-size windows), and how many contexts of a word combine to produce its representation. It also situates static pretrained embeddings (circa 2017) as a common starting point for downstream models that then learn contextual representations.

The treatment is primarily conceptual and motivational: it explains the problem with localist one-hot encodings, the distributional principle (Firth), context-window construction, and the qualitative benefits of dense vectors for expressing similarity. Practical training recipes, count-based alternatives, subword methods, and industrial evaluation/diagnostics are not covered in depth in the course material.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What is the core idea of distributional semantics?  
- Why are one-hot vectors inadequate for measuring word similarity?  
- How is a word's "context" typically defined in the curriculum?

## Identified Gaps
The curriculum gives a strong conceptual foundation but leaves several industry-relevant, practical skills underdeveloped — each is an opportunity to build capabilities that employers frequently seek.

- Practical training and tuning of prediction-based embeddings (missing): Industry expects hands-on competence with skip-gram vs CBOW, negative sampling, window size, subsampling, dimensionality, and optimization choices. This matters for producing embeddings that capture the right semantic relations and scale to large corpora. Priority: (Critical).

- Count-based models and the matrix-factorization view (missing): Understanding co-occurrence matrices, PMI/PPMI weighting, SVD/LSA, and GloVe — and their theoretical connection to prediction-based methods — helps you choose methods that are robust or interpretable for specific data. Priority: (Important).

- Subword/morphology-aware embeddings, OOV handling, evaluation diagnostics, bias auditing and debiasing, retrofitting/specialization, and scalability considerations are all valuable industry skills that are undercovered. Each is important for deploying embeddings in production and for responsible model use. Priority: (Important) for most; (Nice-to-have) for deep deployment engineering like compression/quantization.

## Core Content
This section teaches the most critical missing skills: practical training/tuning of prediction-based embeddings and the count-based/matrix-factorization perspective and their relation to each other.

### What You Need to Learn

Gap 1 — Training and tuning prediction-based embeddings (critical)
- Anchor: Building on the curriculum’s view that word meaning arises from nearby words, prediction-based methods operationalize this by training a model to predict context words from a target (or vice versa), producing dense embeddings as parameters that capture distributional similarity.
- Definition: A prediction-based embedding model (e.g., skip-gram or CBOW) optimizes an objective that encourages word vectors to be predictive of words that appear within a context window; efficient approximations such as negative sampling replace costly full-softmax computations.
- How it works (walkthrough):
  1. Data preparation: tokenize text, build vocabulary, optionally lowercase and normalize; decide on a maximum vocabulary and how to handle rare/OOV tokens.
  2. Context definition: choose a window size (how many tokens to left/right to consider). Larger windows capture broader topical similarity; smaller windows emphasize syntactic/functional relations.
  3. Training objective: choose skip-gram (predict context words given the target) or CBOW (predict target from context). Choose an approximation: negative sampling (sample k negative tokens per positive pair) or hierarchical softmax.
  4. Regularization & sampling: apply subsampling of very frequent words to reduce imbalance; tune embedding dimensionality and learning-rate schedule.
  5. Optimization & monitoring: train with stochastic gradient descent/Adam variants, monitor loss and qualitative nearest-neighbor checks; evaluate on intrinsic/extrinsic metrics.
- Application steps (practical recipe):
  1. Preprocess a representative corpus and build word counts and an index-to-word mapping.
  2. Select window size and decide whether window is symmetric or dynamic; set embedding dimension (a hyperparameter to tune).
  3. Implement or use an optimized library (industry uses libraries like word2vec/FastText implementations) and choose negative sampling with k (e.g., tune k on validation).
  4. Use subsampling to downweight very frequent words; train and periodically inspect nearest neighbors for sample tokens (qualitative sanity checks).
  5. Evaluate embeddings on intrinsic benchmarks (similarity/analogy) and on a downstream validation task relevant to your product.
- Industry example: A search relevance team trains skip-gram embeddings on search query logs and document text, tuning window size and negative sampling to emphasize topical similarity; the resulting vectors allow query-document matching that surfaces "Seattle hotel" pages for "Seattle motel" queries, improving retrieval recall and click-through rates.

Gap 2 — Count-based models and the matrix-factorization view (important)
- Anchor: The curriculum explains that word meaning can be captured by contexts; count-based approaches build an explicit co-occurrence matrix to capture those statistics and then reduce dimensionality to get dense vectors.
- Definition: Count-based models construct a word × context co-occurrence matrix, optionally transform it with PMI or PPMI weighting to emphasize informative co-occurrences, and then apply dimensionality reduction (e.g., truncated SVD / LSA) to obtain dense vectors. GloVe is a related approach that models global co-occurrence statistics with a weighted least-squares objective. Research shows connections between prediction-based models and implicit factorization of such matrices.
- How it works (walkthrough):
  1. Build co-occurrence counts: for each target word, count occurrences of context words within a specified window across the corpus.
  2. Convert counts to association scores like PMI or positive PMI (PPMI), which upweight rare-but-informative co-occurrences and downweight ubiquitous words.
  3. Apply matrix factorization: use truncated SVD to reduce the PMI/PPMI-weighted matrix to a dense low-dimensional representation.
  4. Optionally refine with a model like GloVe that fits a model to the global co-occurrence counts via a weighted regression objective.
- Application steps:
  1. Compute co-occurrence counts on your corpus using the same windowing logic as prediction-based training.
  2. Compute PMI or PPMI matrix entries from counts (conditioning on marginal word/context frequencies).
  3. Run truncated SVD (retain top d singular vectors) to obtain d-dimensional embeddings for words.
  4. Compare these embeddings qualitatively and quantitatively to prediction-based vectors on the tasks you care about.
- Industry example: A data team uses PPMI+SVD to create interpretable vectors for a domain-specific corpus where interpretability and stable representations matter (e.g., legal or medical text). They compare these to prediction-based vectors; if interpretability and stable low-rank structure are desirable, count-based vectors can be favorable. Research (e.g., Levy & Goldberg) formalizes how skip-gram with negative sampling is implicitly factorizing a shifted PMI matrix, clarifying when the two approaches are expected to align.

For remaining gaps (brief summaries):
- Subword/morphology-aware embeddings: FastText uses character n-grams to build vectors for rare or unseen word forms, improving OOV behavior and morphology handling — useful in production (see FastText paper).  
- Evaluation & diagnostics: intrinsic benchmarks (e.g., SimLex-999) and extrinsic downstream testing are essential to validate whether embeddings capture the intended semantic relations.  
- Bias & retrofitting: auditing embeddings for social biases and retrofitting vectors to lexicons (attract/repel constraints) are practical techniques for ethical and task-specific adaptation.  
- Scalability & deployment: memory and nearest-neighbor efficiency matter for production retrieval; consider pruning, quantization, and efficient ANN indices.

### Common Misconceptions
- Misconception: "Static pretrained embeddings are always sufficient for downstream tasks."  
  Why it's wrong: Static vectors capture average (context-free) word usage; some downstream tasks require context-sensitive distinctions and careful tuning of embeddings or additional contextualization. Correct view: Use static embeddings as a strong starting point, but validate on the downstream task and be prepared to adapt or retrain.
- Misconception: "Prediction-based methods and count-based methods are completely different and incomparable."  
  Why it's wrong: There are formal connections (e.g., implicit matrix factorization results) showing prediction-based objectives can approximate factorizing shifted PMI matrices. Correct view: Compare both families empirically for your data and task because their strengths differ depending on corpus size, interpretability needs, and computational constraints.
- Misconception: "OOVs are unavoidable and can't be handled without retraining the whole model."  
  Why it's wrong: Subword methods (character n-grams) and composition from subword units can produce useful vectors for unseen tokens without retraining full vocabulary. Correct view: Plan vocabulary and subword strategies early, especially for morphologically rich domains.

## Industry Context
Roles that value these skills include: NLP Engineer or Research Engineer (building and tuning embedding pipelines), Search/Relevance Engineer (improving query-document matching), and Data Scientist or ML Engineer working on recommendation or semantic retrieval. These roles require turning distributional principles into robust, production-ready embeddings.

Use case (detailed): A large e-commerce company improves product search by training domain-specific embeddings on product titles, descriptions, and query logs. They tune prediction-based embeddings (window, negative sampling) and augment with subword n-grams to handle brand names and misspellings. Embeddings are used to expand queries and compute semantic similarity between queries and product titles; outcome: improved recall and conversion metrics for ambiguous queries (e.g., "running shoe" matching multiple brand variants). Employers hiring for these roles look for skills in preprocessing corpora, selecting and tuning embedding algorithms, evaluating embeddings both intrinsically and on downstream KPIs, and handling OOVs and bias considerations.

When hiring, employers often seek demonstrated experience training embeddings at scale, the ability to choose and justify model families (prediction vs count-based), and practical knowledge of diagnostics and deployment constraints (memory, nearest-neighbor search).

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check
1. What problem do one-hot vectors create for measuring word similarity?  
> Answer: They are orthogonal (no notion of graded similarity), so similar words like "motel" and "hotel" are not close in that representation.

2. According to the curriculum, how is a word's "context" typically defined?  
> Answer: As the set of words appearing nearby within a fixed-size window in text.

3. Conceptual: Why might you choose negative sampling when training a skip-gram model rather than a full softmax?  
> Answer: Negative sampling is an efficient approximation that replaces expensive normalization over the full vocabulary with sampled negatives, making training scalable.

4. Application: Given a small, domain-specific corpus with many rare technical terms, what steps would you take to produce usable embeddings that handle OOVs?  
> Answer: Use subword methods (character n-grams) or FastText-style composition to build vectors for rare/novel tokens, tune window size and dimensionality on a held-out validation task, and validate embeddings with domain-relevant intrinsic/extrinsic evaluations.

### Apply It
Scenario: You work on a search relevance team for a travel site. User logs show many variations ("motel", "inn", "budget hotel") and frequent misspellings. The product team wants a semantic embedding layer to improve query-document matching and to provide suggestions for related searches. You must produce embeddings that (a) capture topical similarity, (b) handle misspellings and rare place names, and (c) can be evaluated before deployment.

Tasks:
- Train prediction-based embeddings on combined query logs and listing text, choosing window size, embedding dimensionality, and negative sampling hyperparameters; document your choices.  
- Incorporate subword (character n-gram) modeling so the system can produce vectors for misspellings and rare tokens.  
- Evaluate embeddings with qualitative nearest-neighbor checks, an intrinsic similarity benchmark (if available), and a small downstream retrieval validation set, then produce a short report with recommended hyperparameters and deployment considerations.

Expected outcome/deliverable:
- A reproducible training recipe (code/config), a set of trained embeddings (with versioning), a validation report showing intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation results plus nearest-neighbor examples (e.g., "motel" neighbors), and deployment notes on OOV handling and memory footprint.

## Key Takeaways
- Curriculum: Distributional semantics frames word meaning by context; "You shall know a word by the company it keeps."  
- Curriculum: One-hot/localist encodings are orthogonal and do not provide graded similarity; dense real-valued vectors encode similarity in geometry.  
- Curriculum: Context windows aggregate many occurrences of a word to build its representation; pretrained static embeddings were historically used as inputs to later contextual models.

- Gap: Training prediction-based embeddings requires practical choices (window size, negative sampling, subsampling, embedding dim) that determine semantic properties and scalability.  
- Gap: Count-based approaches (co-occurrence + PPMI + SVD, GloVe) offer an alternative view; research connects these to prediction-based methods via implicit matrix factorization.  
- Gap: Subword models (FastText), evaluation diagnostics (SimLex, downstream testing), bias auditing, retrofitting, and deployment considerations are essential industry skills beyond the curriculum.

- Integration: Use the curriculum’s distributional principle as the theoretical basis, then apply gap skills (training recipes, count-based understanding, subword handling, evaluation) to produce embeddings that work in real systems.  
- Integration: Empirical comparison and evaluation should guide whether prediction-based or count-based methods (or hybrid approaches) are best for your domain.

## Reflection
- What was the most important thing you learned in this module?  
- Which gap area do you feel least confident about? What would help you strengthen it?  
- How does Distributional Semantics Foundation connect to other topics you have studied?

## Further Reading
- [Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (Mikolov et al., 2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781) (Research Paper) (Intermediate) — Describes the foundational word2vec prediction-based approach and practical considerations for efficient training.  
- [GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation (Pennington et al., 2014)](https://nlp.stanford.edu/pubs/glove.pdf) (Research Paper) (Intermediate) — Presents a global co-occurrence-based model connecting count statistics to dense vectors.  
- [Neural Word Embeddings as Implicit Matrix Factorization (Levy & Goldberg, 2014)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546) (Research Paper) (Advanced) — Explains theoretical connections between prediction-based objectives and matrix factorization of co-occurrence statistics.  
- [Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information (Bojanowski et al., 2017; FastText)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.04606) (Research Paper) (Intermediate) — Describes subword n-gram methods to handle rare tokens and OOVs in embeddings.

Imagine you’re on your first day as an NLP engineer. Your teammate says, “We need embeddings where ‘motel’ sits right next to ‘hotel’, trained on our own data. Can you set that up?” Most graduates know the theory of word vectors—but get stuck right here.

You’ve already learned that word meaning arises from nearby words, and that dense vectors capture graded similarity, unlike orthogonal one-hot encodings. That’s a solid foundation. But to actually build and debug those vectors in practice, you need a bit more: how we train them by predicting context, how count-based alternatives work, and how we handle rare and unseen words.

Let’s start with prediction-based training. Instead of just counting how often words co-occur, we train a small neural model whose job is to predict words from their neighbors. In skip-gram, you take a target word like “motel” and ask the model to predict its surrounding words, like “Seattle”, “cheap”, “airport”. In CBOW, you flip it: use the context to predict the missing target. The key insight here is that the word embeddings are the parameters the model learns so it can make those predictions accurately. Over time, words that share contexts end up with similar vectors.

This matters because industry systems rely heavily on tuned prediction-based models—word2vec-style—to produce embeddings that scale to billions of tokens and reflect the kinds of similarity they care about: topical, functional, or a mix. These models underpin search, recommendation, and a lot of legacy production NLP.

Here’s how it works in practice. You preprocess a big corpus: tokenize, normalize, build your vocabulary. Then you define a symmetric context window—say 5 words on each side. Larger windows capture broad topics; smaller ones capture tighter syntactic roles. Training a full softmax over a huge vocab is too expensive, so you use negative sampling: for each true target–context pair, you sample a few random “fake” contexts and train the model to distinguish real from fake. You also subsample very frequent words like “the” so they don’t dominate training. On the slide’s process flow, you’ll see this as: tokenize corpus, define window, train skip-gram with negative sampling, then tune hyperparameters like embedding dimension, learning rate, window size, and number of negatives. Finally, you inspect nearest neighbors as a sanity check—“motel” should sit near “hotel”, “inn”, “lodging”, not “banana”.

Now let’s shift to count-based factorization. Instead of training a predictor, you first build an explicit word-by-context co-occurrence matrix: how often does each context word appear within your chosen window of each target word? That raw count matrix is huge and skewed, so the key move is to convert counts into association scores like PMI or PPMI, which highlight informative pairs—“motel, Seattle”—and downweight generic ones—“motel, the”. Then you apply truncated SVD: a matrix factorization that compresses this giant PMI matrix into low-dimensional word vectors. If you’re looking at the comparison diagram, that’s the flow from co-occurrence matrix, to PPMI weighting, to SVD, to dense embeddings. These vectors tend to be more stable and interpretable, and can work very well on smaller or domain-specific corpora—for example, legal text, where you might see clear axes for “criminal vs civil” concepts.

Building on that, we need to talk about subword and OOV handling. Pure word-level models assign a single vector per token in the vocabulary. Anything unseen at training time is just “unknown”. In production, that’s a problem: misspellings, rare surnames, new product or place names happen constantly. The key insight here is to represent words as compositions of smaller units, like character n-grams. FastText-style models learn vectors for all 3–6 character chunks inside a word, then sum or average them to form the word’s embedding. That means even if “Seaatle” is misspelled, or a new place name appears, you can still produce a meaningful vector based on its subword pieces, without retraining your entire vocabulary.

Now, a lot of students walk away thinking, “If I just grab a popular pretrained embedding file, I’m done for any task.” But static pretrained vectors capture average, context-free usage and may not reflect your domain, your users’ language, or your fairness constraints. The better mental model is: treat pretrained embeddings as a strong starting point, then validate them on your downstream task, and be ready to adapt—by retraining on your corpus, switching between prediction-based or count-based methods, or adding subword modeling.

Before I wrap up, pause for a moment and think about how you’d choose a context window and a subword strategy if you were training embeddings for noisy social media posts versus for clean legal documents. What would you change, and why?

So here’s what I want you to take away from this. First, prediction-based models like skip-gram with negative sampling turn “predict the context” into useful word embeddings you can tune. Second, count-based approaches—PPMI plus SVD or GloVe—give you an alternative that can be more interpretable and stable. Third, subword modeling is essential if you want your system to cope gracefully with rare words and misspellings. With these tools, you’re much closer to turning the Firth quote into embeddings you can actually deploy.

## Module Overview
Imagine you are building a semantic search feature for a product catalog and need compact vector representations of words to bootstrap downstream models. Training Word2Vec-style embeddings—learning dense vectors so words with similar contexts have similar representations—solves this by turning co-occurrence statistics into parameters you can use for search, clustering, or as inputs to larger models. Industry practice now trains embeddings at web scale, so efficiency and sampling tricks (rather than naive full-softmax training) are essential to make training tractable and produce high-quality vectors. 

This module teaches the canonical curriculum procedures (context-window SGD, mini-batching, softmax-based objectives, and the role of learning rate α) and, critically, closes gaps the course leaves: negative-sampling/NCE alternatives, subsampling and unigram smoothing, and practical implementation patterns for scaling (sampling tables, Hogwild-style updates, batching and optimizer strategies). By the end you will be able to design and implement a production-ready Word2Vec training loop that balances computational cost and embedding quality. 

Ready to move from classroom softmax derivations to an industry-ready training recipe?

## Learning Objectives
1. Explain the Word2Vec training loop and the role of SGD updates after each context window (Curriculum).
2. Derive and interpret gradients for the softmax-based Word2Vec objective and describe how the global learning rate α affects updates (Curriculum).
3. Implement mini-batch gradient descent for windowed context training and integrate a learning-rate schedule (Apply) (Curriculum).
4. Implement Skip-gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) and Noise-Contrastive Estimation (NCE), and compare them to full softmax in terms of computation and optimization behavior (Analyze) (Gap).
5. Apply subsampling of frequent tokens and unigram-distribution smoothing (e.g., exponent 0.75) when constructing negative samples; build or use an O(1) sampling table for efficient negative sampling (Apply) (Gap).
6. Evaluate and choose practical scaling strategies (Hogwild vs. synchronized batching, optimizer choices, checkpointing, and simple numerical-stability practices) for large-corpus embedding training (Evaluate) (Gap).

## Curriculum Coverage
The course introduces word vectors and presents the key idea that word meaning can be represented by dense real-valued vectors. It covers the Word2Vec setup: training on a fixed vocabulary extracted from the corpus, using context windows to form prediction tasks, and deriving the objective gradients for prediction-based embedding learning. The lectures derive the softmax-based view of the Word2Vec objective and show how gradients inform parameter updates.

The curriculum teaches optimization basics relevant to embedding training: performing stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates after each context window, moving to mini-batch gradient descent as a natural extension, computing the full softmax over the vocabulary as the canonical likelihood objective, and controlling step size with a global learning rate α. The course emphasizes gradient-based optimization and provides the theoretical basis (objective and gradient derivations) needed to implement a basic training loop.

Before continuing, make sure you can answer:
- What is the role of a context window in Word2Vec training?
- How does a single SGD update operate after processing one context window?
- What does the learning rate α control in gradient-based optimization?

## Identified Gaps
The curriculum gives a strong theoretical foundation, but industry practice extends beyond full-softmax training and single-rate SGD loops. These gaps are opportunities to build skills that make embeddings usable at scale:

- Missing scalable objectives and sampling alternatives: The course focuses on full softmax but does not teach negative-sampling/NCE or sampled-softmax that are essential to scale to large vocabularies. Why it matters: these methods reduce computational cost by replacing an expensive normalization over the entire vocabulary with a local contrastive objective. Priority: (Critical).

- Sampling and subsampling details: The curriculum omits unigram-distribution smoothing (e.g., exponent 0.75 for negative sampling), fast sampling table construction, and frequent-word subsampling strategies that improve both speed and quality. Why it matters: these heuristics materially affect embedding geometry and training efficiency. Priority: (Important).

- Implementation and scaling practices: There is limited treatment of efficient, parallel implementations (Hogwild-style asynchronous updates, batching strategies, O(1) negative sampling alias tables), learning-rate schedules, and basic numerical-stability or checkpointing practices. Why it matters: production-scale training requires these engineering practices to finish in reasonable time and budget. Priority: (Critical).

- Evaluation and stopping: The curriculum lacks practical validation/evaluation protocols for embeddings (intrinsic vs extrinsic metrics) and early-stopping guidelines. Why it matters: without evaluation practices, hyperparameter tuning and model selection are ad hoc. Priority: (Important).

Each gap is an opportunity to add practical, employable skills building on the course theory.

## Core Content

### What You Need to Learn

Gap 1 — Skip-gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) and Unigram Smoothing (Critical)
- Anchor: Building on the curriculum’s softmax-based Word2Vec objective and SGD updates, SGNS replaces the full-vocabulary softmax with a contrastive objective that trains the model to score true (target, context) pairs higher than sampled negative pairs.
- Definition: SGNS trains by maximizing the probability the model assigns to observed context words while minimizing probability assigned to k sampled negative words; it optimizes a local logistic loss per (target, context) pair rather than normalizing over the whole vocabulary.
- How it works (walkthrough):
  1. For each center (target) word w_t and each context word w_c in its window, treat (w_t, w_c) as a positive pair.
  2. Sample k negative words {n_1,...,n_k} from a noise distribution (commonly the unigram distribution raised to the 0.75 power).
  3. Compute positive score s_pos = u_{w_c} · v_{w_t} and negative scores s_neg_i = u_{n_i} · v_{w_t} (where u are output/context vectors and v are input/center vectors).
  4. Apply logistic losses: L = -log σ(s_pos) - sum_{i=1..k} log σ(-s_neg_i). Compute gradients w.r.t. the involved vectors and update.
- Step-by-step implementation (numbered):
  1. Precompute a negative-sampling distribution P_n(w) ∝ freq(w)^{0.75} and build a fast sampling table (alias or large repeated-array table).
  2. For each sentence, slide the context window; for each center word, enumerate context words and form positive pairs.
  3. For each positive pair, draw k negatives from P_n(w) and compute gradients for v_center, u_pos, and u_neg; apply updates (SGD or mini-batch).
  4. Optionally apply frequent-word subsampling before forming pairs (see next gap), and decay learning rate α over epochs.
- Industry practice example: The original Word2Vec implementation uses SGNS with k between 5–20 negatives, unigram smoothing exponent 0.75, and a large O(1) sampling table; this makes training on billions of tokens feasible while producing high-quality embeddings.

Gap 2 — Subsampling Frequent Tokens, Fast Sampling Tables, and Scaling Strategies (Critical)
- Anchor: The curriculum’s windowed SGD and mini-batching give the per-update mechanics; to scale, you must reduce the number of trivial updates (very frequent words) and make negative sampling constant-time.
- Definitions:
  - Subsampling: probabilistically discarding very frequent words (e.g., "the", "and") during corpus preprocessing to reduce their dominance.
  - Sampling table / alias table: data structures allowing O(1) draws from a discrete distribution such as the smoothed unigram distribution.
  - Hogwild-style updates: asynchronous, lock-free parameter updates across threads to exploit parallelism.
- How it works (walkthrough and steps):
  1. Subsampling frequent words: compute discard probability p(w) = 1 - sqrt(t / f(w)) (or similar; common practice is to reduce frequent-token frequency), and stochastically drop tokens during corpus scanning so fewer trivial pairs are generated.
  2. Build sampling table: create a large array where each token appears proportional to P_n(w); sample by drawing a random index (simple to implement) or implement the alias method for memory-efficient O(1) sampling.
  3. Parallel training patterns:
     - Synchronized mini-batches: accumulate gradients in batches and apply atomic/synchronized updates (good for GPUs).
     - Hogwild/asynchronous: multiple threads update shared vectors without locks (works well for sparse, high-dimensional updates and on CPU implementations).
  4. Learning rate and stability: use a decaying learning rate schedule (linear or exponential decay), monitor loss or downstream intrinsic metrics for early stopping, and apply simple stability measures (gradient clipping if very large updates appear).
- Step-by-step mini-recipe to scale training:
  1. Preprocess corpus with subsampling probabilities to reduce frequent tokens.
  2. Build an O(1) negative-sampling table using P_n(w) ∝ freq^{0.75}.
  3. Train using multiple worker threads; each worker samples sentences, forms pairs, draws negatives from the table, computes local gradients, and applies updates either asynchronously (Hogwild) or into per-worker accumulators to be reduced periodically.
  4. Use a learning-rate schedule and checkpoint parameters regularly.
- Industry practice example: Large-scale CPU-based word2vec implementations (reference codebases) use a large repeated-array sampling table and Hogwild updates to saturate CPU cores, while GPU implementations tend to batch operations and use sampled-softmax APIs where available.

Lesser gaps (brief summaries)
- Hierarchical softmax: alternative exact-likelihood technique using a Huffman tree to reduce softmax cost; matters when you need exact likelihoods — see GloVe/word2vec references to learn more.
- Evaluation & early stopping: know intrinsic tasks (analogies, similarity) and downstream finetuning performance; set aside a small validation set for monitoring.

### Common Misconceptions
- Misconception: "Full softmax is always better than negative sampling."  
  Why wrong: Full softmax optimizes exact likelihood but is computationally infeasible for large vocabularies; SGNS provides a scalable contrastive objective that produces high-quality vectors in practice.  
  Correct: Use full softmax only for small vocabularies or as a reference; use SGNS/NCE/sampled-softmax for scalable training.

- Misconception: "Negative sampling exactly approximates the softmax."  
  Why wrong: Negative sampling is a different objective (contrastive/logistic) and does not equal a full softmax; it yields empirically useful embeddings but the loss landscapes differ.  
  Correct: Treat negative sampling as a practical surrogate that emphasizes distinguishing positives from sampled negatives.

- Misconception: "Dropping frequent words always harms performance."  
  Why wrong: Frequent-word subsampling reduces noise from function words and often improves both efficiency and semantic quality of embeddings.  
  Correct: Use subsampling heuristics judiciously and validate on tasks relevant to your application.

## Industry Context
Roles that value these skills include:
- NLP Engineer / Machine Learning Engineer (embedding training and productionization)
- Research Engineer or Applied ML Researcher (developing and tuning embedding objectives)
- Data Scientist specializing in search or recommendation systems (training vector representations for retrieval)

Real-world use case (detailed): An e-commerce company wants semantic product search that understands user queries beyond exact keywords. They collect a large corpus of product titles and descriptions and train word embeddings via SGNS with unigram smoothing and frequent-word subsampling. Efficient negative sampling (O(1) sampling table) and multi-threaded Hogwild updates let them train on hundreds of millions of tokens in a few hours. The resulting embeddings feed a retrieval pipeline that improves relevant-first ranking and increases conversion rates. Employers in such settings look for the ability to implement scalable training loops, tune sampling/subsampling hyperparameters, and validate embeddings with both intrinsic metrics and downstream business metrics.

When hiring, employers ask for practical skills: implementing SGNS or sampled-softmax, building efficient sampling data structures, choosing and tuning learning-rate schedules, and demonstrating experience with parallel training and basic evaluation protocols.

## Practice & Review

### Quick Check
1. What does an SGD update after each context window do in Word2Vec training?  
> Answer: It computes gradients of the objective (softmax-based or contrastive) for the observed center-context pairs in that window and updates the involved vectors using the learning rate α.

2. What role does the global learning rate α play during embedding training?  
> Answer: α scales the magnitude of parameter updates from gradients; it controls convergence speed and stability and is commonly decayed over time.

3. Why is negative sampling used instead of full softmax for large vocabularies?  
> Answer: Negative sampling replaces the expensive normalization over the entire vocabulary with a local contrastive loss computed against a small set of sampled negatives, drastically reducing computation per update.

4. Design element: How would you combine mini-batch gradient descent (curriculum) with SGNS (gap) in a single training loop?  
> Answer: Accumulate several (center, context) positive pairs into a mini-batch, for each positive draw k negatives from the sampling table, vectorize score computations across pairs and negatives, compute gradients for the batch, and apply a single batched parameter update (optionally synchronized across workers).

### Apply It
Scenario: You are given a 200M-token product descriptions corpus and need to produce 300-dimensional word embeddings for downstream search. You must finish training within available compute (a 16-CPU machine) and produce vectors that improve a keyword-matching baseline. Use Word2Vec-style training but scale it for the corpus.

Tasks:
- Preprocess and subsample frequent tokens to reduce trivial pairs; build a negative-sampling table using unigram smoothing with exponent 0.75.
- Implement an SGNS training loop that uses multiple threads with Hogwild-style asynchronous updates; choose k negatives per positive and a decaying learning-rate schedule.
- Validate embeddings on an intrinsic similarity set and a held-out retrieval development set; checkpoint models regularly and pick the best checkpoint by downstream retrieval performance.

Expected outcome/deliverable:
- A trained 300-dimensional embedding file (word → vector), training logs showing loss and validation metrics, and a short report comparing baseline retrieval vs. embedding-augmented retrieval with hyperparameters used.

## Key Takeaways
- Curriculum: Word2Vec-style embedding training uses context windows to form supervised-like prediction tasks and derives gradients for learning dense vectors.
- Curriculum: The canonical training loop uses SGD updates for each window or mini-batches, computes a softmax-based objective over the vocabulary, and controls step size with a learning rate α.
- Curriculum: Understanding the objective and its gradients is essential to implement and reason about embedding updates.

- Gap: In practice, full softmax is usually replaced by SGNS/NCE/sampled-softmax to make training computationally feasible on large vocabularies (critical).
- Gap: Practical sampling choices matter — frequent-word subsampling and unigram smoothing (e.g., exponent 0.75) materially affect both training speed and embedding quality (important).
- Gap: Efficient implementations (O(1) sampling tables, Hogwild or batched parallelism), learning-rate schedules, checkpointing, and simple stability measures are required to scale to industry-sized corpora (critical).

- Integration: Combine curriculum knowledge (objectives, gradients, SGD) with gap techniques (SGNS, sampling tables, subsampling, scaling strategies) to build production-ready embedding training pipelines.
- Integration: Validating embeddings requires both intrinsic checks (similarity/analogy) and downstream evaluation to ensure improvements translate to application performance.

## Reflection
- What was the most important thing you learned in this module?
- Which gap area do you feel least confident about? What would help you strengthen it?
- How does Training Procedure for Embeddings connect to other topics you have studied?

## Further Reading
- [Efficient Estimation of Word Representations in Vector Space (Mikolov et al., 2013)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781) (Research Paper) — (Intermediate)  
  Learn the original SGNS formulation, subsampling heuristic, and unigram smoothing recommendations.

- [Noise-contrastive estimation: A new estimation principle for unnormalized statistical models (Gutmann & Hyvärinen, 2010)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/volume13/gutmann12a/gutmann12a.pdf) (Research Paper) — (Advanced)  
  Understand the theoretical foundations of NCE, an alternative to full softmax for unnormalized models.

- [word2vec GitHub repository (reference implementation)](https://github.com/tmikolov/word2vec) (Tutorial / Code) — (Intermediate)  
  See practical implementation choices (sampling tables, multithreading) used in a reference C implementation.

- [sampled_softmax_loss — TensorFlow documentation](https://www.tensorflow.org/api_docs/python/tf/nn/sampled_softmax_loss) (Documentation) — (Intermediate)  
  Practical API reference if you implement sampled-softmax on GPU frameworks.

Most students think they understand skip-gram once they’ve seen the softmax equation. But what if I told you that, in industry, that version basically never ships, and without one extra idea it simply doesn’t scale to real vocabularies?

You’ve already learned about skip-gram with center vectors v, context vectors u, a dot product between them, and a softmax that predicts nearby words using SGD. That’s a solid foundation, but there are two critical extensions your course didn’t really dig into: negative sampling to make training actually feasible, and subword skip-gram so rare and unseen words still get good embeddings.

Let’s start with negative sampling. Intuitively, instead of asking, “Given this center word, how probable is every word in the whole vocabulary?” we flip it into, “Given this center word, which words look like real neighbors and which look fake?” So each training step becomes a tiny binary classification game: one true context word versus a few randomly sampled “noise” words.

Why does this matter? A full softmax means, for every training pair, you touch every single word vector in the vocabulary. With hundreds of thousands of words and billions of tokens, that’s hopelessly slow. Negative sampling is the trick that lets Word2Vec-style models train at web scale on ordinary hardware.

Here’s how it works. For each observed center–context pair, say center “hotel” and context “Seattle”, you first treat that as a positive example. Then you sample k negative words from a noise distribution, often proportional to unigram frequency to the 0.75 power. That tends to pick common words, but not so aggressively that “the” dominates. If you’re looking at the slide, you can see the process flow: we start from the corpus pair, we sample negatives, we compute dot products, we apply a contrastive loss, and then we do an SGD update. Concretely, you increase the dot product u_Seattleᵀ v_hotel, pulling “Seattle” closer to “hotel,” and you decrease u_nᵀ v_hotel for each negative word n, pushing those away. The key insight is: you still have the same v and u vectors and the same notion of similarity via dot product — you’ve just replaced the expensive full softmax with a cheap sampled objective that only touches a handful of vectors per step.

Now let’s shift to subword skip-gram. Classic skip-gram gives each word its own vector. That breaks down for rare inflected forms, misspellings, and morphologically rich languages where you see thousands of variants of the same stem. Subword skip-gram fixes this by building a word’s embedding from character n‑grams, so words can share pieces. On the slide’s comparison diagram, instead of a single ID lookup for the whole word, you see the word broken into character n‑grams and then recomposed into a vector. For a word like “banking”, you might use 3–6 character n‑grams such as “ban”, “ank”, “nki”, “kin”, “ing”. You assign vectors to each of these n‑grams. To get the word vector for “banking”, you sum or average its n‑gram vectors. Then you plug that composed vector into the usual skip-gram training loop, typically with negative sampling. The model no longer learns “banking” in isolation; it learns reusable pieces that also appear in “bank”, “banker”, or “unbanked”. The key benefit is that a word you’ve never seen before can still get a meaningful embedding, as long as its character n‑grams were seen during training. That’s exactly why subword skip-gram, like fastText, is still widely used in production for noisy text, user queries, and morphologically rich languages.

Now, a lot of students hear about negative sampling and think, “Oh, that’s a different model — it replaces skip-gram.” But here’s the thing: it doesn’t change the representation or the goal at all. You still learn center and context vectors, and you still want high dot products for true neighbors and low ones for unrelated words. Negative sampling is just a scalable way to approximate the same objective without computing a full softmax.

Before I wrap up, pause for a moment and think about this: if you had to train embeddings on a billion-token corpus with lots of rare word forms, how would you combine negative sampling and subword skip-gram to make training both scalable and robust to those rare words?

So here’s what I want you to take away from this. First, negative sampling turns the softmax skip-gram objective into many tiny contrastive classification problems so you can train on massive vocabularies. Second, subword skip-gram composes word vectors from character n‑grams, giving good representations even for rare or unseen forms. And third, both ideas keep the original skip-gram core — center and context vectors, dot products, and SGD — but make it practical for real-world NLP. Mastering these puts you much closer to how embeddings are actually built and used in industry.
